title: Peter Kim
text:
Hello!
I am from South Korea but moved to Vancouver after turning eight. I studied Cognitive Systems (Language stream) for my undergradate program at the University of British Columbia, and conducted Neuroscience research at the UBC Interactive Mind and Movement Lab before joining MDS.
I hope to build a stronger technical foundation through the MDS program so that I can continue working responsibly and effectively with data in the healthcare sector, especially in Neuroimaging.

Data: gapminder by Jennifer Bryan (CC0), read from the package’s TSV file on GitHub. Based on free material from GAPMINDER.ORG, CC-BY LICENSE.
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jennybc/gapminder/refs/heads/main/inst/extdata/gapminder.tsv"
gapminder = pd.read_csv(url, sep="\t")
Setting up, loading required libraries. The dataset is loaded from GitHub through a URL. Internet connection is required for loading the data.
gapminder.info()

# Coverage: how many countries, which years, any missing values?
coverage = pd.DataFrame({
    "n_rows": [len(gapminder)],
    "n_countries": [gapminder["country"].nunique()],
    "first_year": [gapminder["year"].min()],
    "last_year": [gapminder["year"].max()],
    "missing_values": [gapminder.isna().sum().sum()],
})
display(coverage)

# Does every country have all survey years? (needed to compare 1952 with 2007)
(
    gapminder.groupby("country")["year"]
    .count()
    .value_counts()
    .rename_axis("years_per_country")
    .reset_index(name="n_countries")
)

First, we explore the data. The dataset has 1,704 rows and six columns: country, continent, year, life expectancy, population, and GDP per capita. It covers 142 countries surveyed every five years from 1952 to 2007, and there are no missing values. The last table confirms that every country appears in all 12 survey years, so each country has both a 1952 and a 2007 value to compare. GDP per capita is measured in inflation-adjusted international dollars, which makes values comparable across countries and years.
# One row per country, one column per year, values = GDP per capita
gdp_wide = gapminder.pivot(index="country", columns="year", values="gdpPercap")

# Growth from 1952 to 2007 for every country
growth = pd.DataFrame({
    "continent": gapminder.groupby("country")["continent"].first(),
    "gdp_1952": gdp_wide[1952],
    "gdp_2007": gdp_wide[2007],
})
growth["growth_pct"] = (growth["gdp_2007"] / growth["gdp_1952"] - 1) * 100

# Top 5 countries by percentage growth
top5 = growth.sort_values("growth_pct", ascending=False).head(5).round(1)

The five countries with the highest growth are Equatorial Guinea, Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore, and Botswana. Equatorial Guinea displays the largest growth by far: its GDP per capita in 2007 was about 32 times its 1952 level. Taiwan and South Korea each grew roughly 23 to 24 times, Singapore about 20 times, and Botswana about 15 times. Three of the five are in East and Southeast Asia and two are in Africa. Most of these countries started from a low GDP per capita in 1952; Singapore started higher and still ranks fourth.
top5_data = gapminder[gapminder["country"].isin(top5.index)].copy()
top5_data["gdp_index"] = top5_data["gdpPercap"] / top5_data["country"].map(growth["gdp_1952"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
for country in top5.index:
    country_data = top5_data[top5_data["country"] == country]
    ax.plot(country_data["year"], country_data["gdp_index"], marker="o", label=country)
ax.axhline(1, color="grey", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("GDP per capita relative to 1952 (1952 = 1)")
ax.legend(title="Country")
plt.show()







Figure 1: GDP per capita relative to 1952 for the five countries with the highest growth, 1952–2007. A value of 10 means ten times the 1952 level.
Figure 1 shows two different routes to the top five. Taiwan, South Korea, and Singapore grew steadily from the 1960s onward, with growth building on itself over four decades. Botswana followed a similar path starting in the late 1960s. Equatorial Guinea looks very different: its GDP per capita barely moved for forty years, and nearly all of its growth came after 1992, when it rose from about three times its 1952 level to over thirty times by 2007.

title: Python Computational Post:
text:
Conclusion
Equatorial Guinea, Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore, and Botswana had the highest growth in GDP per capita between 1952 and 2007.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
New backpack from orientation!


My first week at MDS picked up quite quickly. The orientation flooded my mind with information, and though I knew this program was growing, I was quite surprised at how many members this cohort contained. Despite the size of the cohort, I was already meeting wonderful people I would walk with throughout my time at MDS.
The first week of classes flew by even faster. Many assignments to submit, several ways to submit them, and a growing list of things to remember for each class. But by the end of the week, I was feeling accomplished at how much I had learned already. It felt like I learned more in one week than my past summer before the program.
Now, I’m feeling excited to continue learning and have a chance to test it with the upcoming quizzes. Hopefully that gives me a better understanding of how each block runs throughout the program!

title: R Computational Post: Continent Life Expectancy
text:
Data: gapminder R package by Jennifer Bryan (CC0). Based on free material from GAPMINDER.ORG, CC-BY LICENSE.

library(gapminder)
library(tidyverse)

Setting up, loading required libraries.

glimpse(gapminder)

Rows: 1,704
Columns: 6
$ country   <fct> "Afghanistan", "Afghanistan", "Afghanistan", "Afghanistan", …
$ continent <fct> Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, Asia, …
$ year      <int> 1952, 1957, 1962, 1967, 1972, 1977, 1982, 1987, 1992, 1997, …
$ lifeExp   <dbl> 28.801, 30.332, 31.997, 34.020, 36.088, 38.438, 39.854, 40.8…
$ pop       <int> 8425333, 9240934, 10267083, 11537966, 13079460, 14880372, 12…
$ gdpPercap <dbl> 779.4453, 820.8530, 853.1007, 836.1971, 739.9811, 786.1134, …

# Coverage: how many countries, which years, any missing values?
data_explore <- gapminder |>
  summarise(
    n_rows = n(),
    n_countries = n_distinct(country),
    first_year = min(year),
    last_year = max(year),
    missing_values = sum(is.na(gapminder))
  )

data_explore

# A tibble: 1 × 5
  n_rows n_countries first_year last_year missing_values
   <int>       <int>      <int>     <int>          <int>
1   1704         142       1952      2007              0


First, we explore the data. The question I want to answer is: “How much life expectancy increase do we observe per continent?” This would be over the course of the dataset’s data collection range, which is shown to be 55 years, from 1952 to 2007.

# Countries per continent (counted in one year so each country appears once)
gap_continent <- gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  count(continent, name = "n_countries")

gap_continent

# A tibble: 5 × 2
  continent n_countries
  <fct>           <int>
1 Africa             52
2 Americas           25
3 Asia               33
4 Europe             30
5 Oceania             2


Checking how many countries there are per continent.

# Median life expectancy per continent per survey year (used in the figure)
lifeexp_by_continent <- gapminder |>
  group_by(continent, year) |>
  summarise(
    median_lifeExp = median(lifeExp),
    n_countries = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Change in the median from the first to the last survey year
lifeexp_change <- lifeexp_by_continent |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(
    median_1952 = median_lifeExp[year == 1952],
    median_2007 = median_lifeExp[year == 2007],
    gain_years = median_2007 - median_1952
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(gain_years))

lifeexp_change

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  continent median_1952 median_2007 gain_years
  <fct>           <dbl>       <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Asia             44.9        72.4       27.5
2 Americas         54.7        72.9       18.2
3 Africa           38.8        52.9       14.1
4 Europe           65.9        78.6       12.7
5 Oceania          69.3        80.7       11.5


This dataframe shows the median life expectancy in each continent in 1952, and in 2007 which is 55 years later. It also shows how much the life expectancy incrased over the period of 55 years.

ggplot(lifeexp_by_continent, aes(x = year, y = median_lifeExp, colour = continent)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Median life expectancy (years)",
    colour = "Continent"
  )







Figure 1: Median life expectancy by continent, 1952–2007.





To visualize our results, his is a line graph showing the growth in median life expectancy by continent. It plots the We observe that Oceania maintains the highest median life expectancy, but also very high growth in Asia, to almost catch up to the Americas.

title: About
text: Entering into the Cognitive Systems program at UBC for my undergraduate program, I knew I wanted to work interchangably between multiple domains such as Linguistics and Computer Science, but I was unsure what that would practically look like. I realized through my research experience (introduced below) that a particular way this could be done was through research in healthcare involving machine learning with neural data. Since then, my research interest has been in neuroimaging methods, and this program is a significant part of this journey.

title: About
text:
Why data science?
In my final year of undergrad, I joined the Interactive Mind and Movement Lab for a capstone project that involved empirically comparing neuroimaging methods for their effectiveness and validity. Through this project I quickly realized a solid technical foundation was essential for conducting responsible, informed research that could meaningfully contribute to furthering these methods. That realization has drawn me to data science as a displine and the MDS program, which aims to establish responsible and reproducible workflows involving data.
